questions.subject: ENVIRONMENT
questions.microTopic: Global warming, climate change, and international frameworks
questions.microtag: What are, Throw light, Marine heat waves, Ecosystem
questions.questionText: What are marine heat waves? Throw light on its impact on marine ecosystem and coastal communities.

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • In the introduction, explain marine heat waves briefly.
• In the body, throw light on their impact on marine ecosystems and coastal communities.
• Conclude by highlighting some measures for mitigation and adaptation. | | --- | Marine heat waves (MHWs) are extreme weather events linked with marine areas. They occur where the surface temperature of a particular region of the sea rises by 3 to 4 ℃ above the average temperature for at least five days. Two main drivers of marine heat waves are: 1. Surface heat flux: Heating of sea surface due to presence of an atmospheric high-pressure system above a region of water for an extended period. 2. Advection: Movement of warmer waters into the region by ocean currents. They have severe impact on marine ecosystems and coastal communities, as discussed: 1. a) Disruption of food webs due to invasive alien species, harmful algal blooms; b) amplify the risk of other ocean stressors like acidification, deoxygenation; c) can cause incidents of mass mortalities. This can happen when the threshold for thermal tolerance is breached or due to increase in hypoxic zones e.g. (“fish kills” in Gulf of Thailand and Gulf of Mexico). 2. a) Loss of ocean biodiversity due to habitat destruction (kelp forests, seagrass meadows, coral reefs are most sensitive to MHWs); b) forced changes in species’ behaviour (altering migration patterns). This increases the risk of harm to marine species (e.g. increase in whale and dolphin stranding in the South Pacific Ocean in January 2024). 3. a) Impact on aquaculture and fisheries (death or reduced productivity of economically important species like lobsters and snow crabs). It has a cascading effect on livelihoods and food security; b) harms regional tourism. 4. a) Disruption of water cycle (increased evaporation). This can cause hydrological (floods, droughts) and meteorological (wildfires, heatwaves) disasters on the land; b) frequent MHWs in the Indian Ocean is altering the patterns of monsoon rains (IITM study). This can severely impact agriculture and allied activities, for e.g. MHWs in Bay of Bengal in June 2023 caused extreme rainfall in usually arid north-western part of India. 5. a) Can ‘supercharge’ the heat and moisture exchanges between sea and air, which could intensify tropical cyclones (e.g. Cyclone Remal). This can have devastating consequences for coastal communities (e.g. loss of life and property) c) contributes to sea-level rise (due to thermal expansion of water), which can lead to coastal erosion, flooding, etc. An analysis published in Nature Climate Change has pointed out a 240 per cent increase in the average number of marine heatwave (MHW) days in the summers of 2023-24. It is important to develop better response plans and adaptation and intervention approaches as they intensify under climate change. Measures to reduce global carbon emissions and slow down ocean warming can counteract their impact and build ocean resilience. (432 words) Additional reading: https://forumias.com/blog/marine-heatwaves-mhws/ Rapid warming over last 2 years likely caused 240% increase in marine heatwaves globally: Study Extra marks/content differentiation: Previous studies have shown that the Indian Ocean has warmed at a rate of 1.2°C per century during 1950-2020. Between 2020 and 2100, climate models predict warming at a rate of 1.7°C-3.8°C per century. The effects are expected to be more pronounced in the northwestern Indian Ocean including the Arabian Sea.

questions.microTopic: Disaster Management: Preparedness, resilience, and vulnerability frameworks
questions.microtag: What is, How, Describe, Mention, Disaster resilience, Sendai Framework
questions.questionText: What is disaster resilience? How is it determined? Describe various elements of a resilience framework. Also mention the global targets of Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015-2030).

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer with a brief definition of disaster resilience.
• In the body, first explain how it is determined.
• Next, describe the various elements of a resilience framework.
• Lastly, mention the global targets of Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015-30).
• Conclude by highlighting the significance of recent changes in the Disaster Management Act for disaster resilience. | | --- | According to UNDRR, disaster resilience means the ability of communities to anticipate, accommodate, and recover from disasters while maintaining essential functions. It is determined by the degree to which the social system is capable of enhancing its capacity to learn from past disasters. This leads to better future protection and improved risk reduction measures. A disaster resilient framework consists of diverse elements as discussed: 1. a) Hazard identification, exposure mapping and vulnerability assessment across social, economic and environmental dimensions; b) planning for the disaster through mitigation (earthquake proofing of building codes) and adaptation measures (drought resilient crop varieties). 2. a) Infrastructure evaluation, especially critical infrastructure (health, communication); b) development of infrastructural (cyclone shelters) and institutional capacity (National Disaster Management Plan); c) capacity building of the community (awareness generation, training, knowledge creation through NIDM) 3. a) Augmentation of the resource base of the economy (financial, technological) to deal with disaster comprehensively; b) ensuring availability of human capital (trained personnel, social networks, social cohesion and trust, local leadership); c) strengthening social security architecture (e.g. risk coverage through insurance). 4. a) Mounting an effective response to the disaster through a whole of society (civil society organizations, volunteer groups) and a whole of government approach (multi-agency coordination); b) effective rehabilitation and recovery from the disaster (Build Back Better approach). The Sendai Framework is the successor of the Hyogo Framework for Action and outlines 7 global targets to be achieved by 2030: I. Substantially reduce: (a) Global disaster mortality (lower average per 100,000 global mortality). (b)The number of affected people (lower average global figure per 100,000). (c) Direct disaster economic loss in relation to global GDP. (d) Damage to critical infrastructure and disruption of basic services (health and education) II. Substantially increase: (e) Number of countries with national and local DRR strategies by 2020. (f) International cooperation to developing countries to complement their national actions. (g) Availability of and access to multi-hazard early warning systems and disaster risk information and assessments. The Disaster Management (Amendment) Act, 2025 marks a significant step towards mainstreaming disaster resilience in development planning. It is expected to go a long way in building a disaster-resilient Bharat. (326 words) Additional reading: Strengthening telecom networks ensures resilience during disasters |ForumIAS Why India needs to build disaster resilience in its critical infrastructure | Explained News - The Indian Express Extra marks/content differentiation: 1. Quotes: “When it comes to disaster management, a proactive approach is always better than a reactive one”- Prime Minister Narendra Modi 2. International Best Practices: In Chile, innovative stormwater management systems and alluvial flood protection schemes have been designed to address flood issues by integrating future climate projections into their design. These systems incorporate updated geotechnical, structural, and hydraulic information combined with natural water retention methods, effectively reducing the impact of climate-induced flood events in the cities. 3. Best practices from India: Real-time monitoring and early warning systems such as cloud-based E-Abhas software have been developed by NHPC Limited. They provide timely warnings against flood risks, enabling governments and communities to take appropriate actions. The implementation of the EWS has significantly enhanced disaster preparedness and response capabilities in regions vulnerable to floods.
